1:
Two of them open not on the verse but on whether the letter is genuine, and they frame the question differently. Barnes reports the ancient doubt and is careful about its extent: the sole ground was ever the authorship, the historian who lists the disputed books puts this one among those spoken against without himself disbelieving it, one father records that many denied it to Peter because the style differs from the first epistle, and another writes that Peter left one epistle acknowledged and that it may be granted he wrote a second, since it is doubted of. Clarke, following a German critic, presses the matter to a dilemma. The writer states that he is writing to the same people as before, calls himself by both names, and says he was present at the transfiguration; so the conjecture that some later bishop of the same name wrote it is inadmissible, and no alternative remains but that the apostle wrote it or that it is a forgery in his name.

The first word of the letter then becomes evidence, and three make three different things of it. Ellicott prefers the more Jewish form of the name and argues from it in both directions at once: as the Jewish form it points to a Jewish Christian for author, and as an unusual form it shows that the writer, if he is not the apostle, is at any rate no slavish imitator. Henry explains the same choice pastorally, that the name given at circumcision was left out of the first letter and is restored here lest Jewish believers, being zealous for the law, should grow jealous of an apostle who seemed to drop it. Calvin looks at the same fact and declines to explain it, saying simply that why he called himself Peter in the first epistle and Simeon Peter here does not appear. Robertson keeps to the manuscripts, which are divided, and notes that both forms are used indifferently of the same man in the Maccabean history. Ellicott adds the comparison that gives his argument its weight: in the earlier letter, approaching communities that might have thought themselves another apostle's, the writer suppressed everything personal and called himself only Peter and an apostle, whereas here, coming a second time to people who know him, he adds the personal designations.

On the two titles Gill distinguishes the servant of Christ from the servant of sin, Satan or man, and takes the second name for what Christ gave him with a view to his future firmness. Calvin makes the first title wider than the second, since it covers every minister holding public office in the Church, while the apostleship is a higher rank — so that the writer marks himself out as made an apostle by the Lord and not merely reckoned among the ministers.

The description of the readers' faith is where the sense turns. Robertson notes that the compound adjective can mean either equal in value or equal in honour, that the second is the usual force of this particular word, and that the faith so described is therefore like in honour and privilege with that of any apostle. Wesley says the same thing from the other end, that the faith of those who have not seen is equally precious with the faith of those who saw the Lord in the flesh. Calvin calls it no common gift that all the elect were called to one and the same faith, faith being the chief good of man. Robertson also observes that the verb for obtaining is the word for obtaining by lot, and Wesley draws the conclusion, that it came not by their own works but by free grace — as does the clause about righteousness, which he takes of both the active and the passive obedience, and by which alone he says the justice of God is satisfied.
2:
The phrase about knowledge is construed four ways. Ellicott would render the preposition in rather than through, since it marks the sphere in which the thing happens, and notes that two older English versions did so; the noun is a compound implying a fuller knowledge than the plain word, though no English term quite fits. Robertson agrees and supplies a motive, that full knowledge is urged here, as in another epistle, against heretical claims to a special knowledge. Calvin allows that the preposition may mean either through or with, and is more disposed to the first. Clarke takes the noun as acknowledgment rather than knowledge, and draws a practical inference: those who know Christ and will not own him before men get no multiplication of grace and peace. Wesley calls it the divine and experimental knowledge.

Whose power is meant divides them by degrees of confidence. Ellicott says flatly that the pronoun refers to Jesus our Lord, and notes that the adjective occurs in the New Testament only here and in one other place; Robertson refers it to Christ as well and makes the reference an argument, since the one who has divine power is the one already called God in the first verse. Gill weighs the Father and the Son and settles on the Son, but only because he is the nearer antecedent. Ellicott also argues from epistolary usage that the third verse must not depend on the second, since in the canonical letters the address never runs past the blessing, the one exception being framed so as almost to prove the rule; and he reads the writer's haste to reach his subject as characteristic of the man.

What is given, and to whom, then separates two pairs. Barnes confines the life in question to the life of religion, the life of the soul imparted by the gospel, while Wesley expressly includes the present natural life alongside the continuance and increase of the spiritual. Clarke narrows the recipients: taking the verb as hath gifted us, he applies it to what the Spirit gave the apostles — knowledge of the doctrine, power to preach it, wisdom for every occasion, miraculous powers — where the others take the gift as made to Christians at large.

The relative at the fourth verse has no agreed antecedent. Ellicott says it is the glory and virtue and not the things pertaining to life, while allowing the other is possible; Robertson calls the glory and virtue probable and lists the alternatives without deciding; Calvin locates the difficulty exactly, that what is said does not suit the glory conferred on us, and holds that reading it of God's own glory and power removes the ambiguity — supporting this with a lexical claim, that the second word never means power in classical or biblical Greek. On which promises are meant, Ellicott and Clarke disagree outright. Ellicott says they are not the promises of the older covenant that Christ should come, but those of the newer that he should come again, the certainty of his return being the point. Clarke says the Jews were distinguished by their promises and that Gentile readers are told they have received the same, everything given to the Jews except the settlement in the land.

On the last clause Cyril gives a reading nobody else gives. Partaking of the Body and Blood makes a man of one body and blood with Christ, so that Christ is borne in us and distributed through our members — and it is thus, he says, quoting this verse, that we become partakers of the divine nature. Wesley makes the same phrase moral and mystical instead, a renewal in the image of God and a communion by which we dwell in God and God in us. Gill takes the promises to be at Christ's disposal, as being all in him.
5:
The opening words are read in opposite directions. Ellicott calls the received English quite indefensible and would have for this very reason, the more so because the common rendering hides a parallel with the earlier epistle; Robertson construes the Greek the same way, and Wesley gives the sense outright, because God has given you so great blessings. Clarke turns it about into a concession — notwithstanding what God has done for you, and in order that you may not receive his grace in vain — which makes the diligence a safeguard rather than a consequence. Barnes says only that something must be supplied to complete the sentence, and refers it back to the third verse.

What the diligence contributes divides them by a hair that matters. Wesley notes that the verb is uncommon and means bringing in over and above, so that our diligence follows the gift of God and is followed by an increase of it, good works doing nothing of themselves and nothing being done without them. Ellicott says the same spatially, that the diligence is brought in alongside God's gifts and promises as our contribution in answer to his, everything having been made possible and nothing yet done. Calvin makes it plainer still: putting off the corruption in us is arduous and of immense labour, so no place is left for sloth, and the effort is to be made evident to all. Robertson borrows a sentence to the same effect, that the soul of religion is the practical part, and remarks that the exact phrase turns up on an ancient inscription, which he calls a curious coincidence.

Whether the virtues form a chain is the substantial question, and four answers stand side by side. Clarke and Wesley both hear a dance in the verb: it means to lead up hand in hand, as the chorus did with joined hands, and Wesley adds that each preceding grace leads to the following in a beautiful order, and that the later are to be superadded without losing the former. Ellicott denies the preposition that would make a chain at all — the reading should be in your faith supply virtue, not to it, and the error entered from one English version while all the rest are right. Calvin grants that supplying to faith is adding to faith and then withholds the inference, saying there is no proper gradation here in the sense. Barnes enters a caution of his own, that the verses do not mean the graces are to be acquired one after another in the order named.

On the particular virtues the readings are practical. Clarke takes the first not as goodness but as courage or fortitude, to enable a man to profess the faith before men in a time of persecution, and Wesley agrees, making it that by which enemies and difficulties are conquered and whatever faith dictates is executed. Clarke reads the knowledge that follows as the wisdom which increases faith and keeps courage from degenerating into rashness. Gill defines temperance as avoiding excess in food and drink and all impure desire, adds that it may take in abstinence from things indifferent when a weaker brother's peace is at stake, and identifies a target for the whole clause: it seems levelled at a party who made salvation depend on knowledge however impure the life. Henry stands back and states the purpose of the letter, that this is the chief thing intended in it — the readers have obtained precious faith already, which is a very good beginning and not to be rested in as though they were perfect; and he draws the pastoral rule that we should exhort those we pray for, and stir them up to use the means for what we ask God to give them, since without all diligence no ground is gained in the work of holiness.
8:
Five agree that the received English of the eighth verse says one thing twice. Clarke puts it hardest, that barren and unfruitful convey the same idea and that the first word properly means idle or inactive, which removes the tautology and restores the sense; Ellicott agrees and observes that three older English versions had it right; Barnes says the marginal reading expresses the original more accurately; Robertson notes both adjectives carry the same privative; Wesley gives slothful and unfruitful. Ellicott adds two smaller corrections, that the verb for being in you implies a permanent and not a momentary possession, and that the second verb means strictly to multiply. Calvin turns the clause into a test: the knowledge of Christ is an efficacious thing and a living root that bears fruit, so that men who boast of knowing him without love and patience glory falsely. Wesley presses the same test on the reader's own history — if there is less watchfulness since pardon than there was before it, and less obedience than when remission was still being sought, then the man is both slothful and unfruitful. Barnes reads the verse as encouragement instead, since nowhere is there more of it than in the attempt to become eminent in piety. Gill refers the graces to the Spirit, who works in believers both to will and to do, and takes the promised abundance of the last verse as grace for present trials and admission at the end.

At the ninth verse Barnes explains the rare word for the defect of sight: it means to contract the eyelids or to blink, and so to be short-sighted, the man seeing what lies near and having no clear apprehension of what is further off.

The tenth verse is where the traditions part, and four accounts of making the calling and election sure stand side by side. Calvin takes the surety as evidence rather than cause: a good conscience and integrity of life answering to the profession is one proof that we have really been elected and not called in vain — and he notes that the calling is named first though it is the later of the two, election being of greater weight. Barnes reads it as assurance, the appeal resting on the uncertainty that low attainment throws over a man's own salvation and on the condemnation awaiting one found destitute at the end. Clarke reverses the order outright, making election the being chosen to be God's people in consequence of obeying the heavenly calling, and holds that both will prove ultimately unprofitable unless what has been received is held fast by adding the graces. Wesley states the same conditionality as a promise with an edge — cast not away these inestimable benefits, and if you are thus diligent to make your election firm you shall never finally fall. Ellicott stands between them with a definition rather than a doctrine, calling and election being two aspects of one fact, the first God's invitation and the second the distinction that invitation makes between those called and those not; Robertson divides them the same way, as the invitation and the acceptance.

Two textual notes attach to the same verse and are judged oppositely. Calvin reports that some copies add by good works, says there is no sufficient authority for introducing the phrase, and adds that it changes nothing since the pronoun already looks back to the graces named. Ellicott reports the same insertion from one of the best manuscripts and several versions, and says that although the words want authority they give the right sense. Clarke supplies a variant nobody else mentions, that one great codex reads consolation in place of calling. Robertson notes the double negative that makes the promise of not stumbling emphatic, and Wesley observes that the writer uses the address brethren nowhere else in either letter but at this one exhortation.
12:
The opening promise is corrected by two. Ellicott says the right reading gives not a refusal to be negligent but a positive undertaking, I shall be sure to remind you; Robertson construes it the same way, as a settled purpose to be ready in future as in the past, and denies that the construction is merely a periphrastic future. Calvin explains why an apology is needed: to remind men often of one thing looks like distrusting their memory, so the writer excuses himself on the ground that in a matter of such greatness admonitions are never superfluous and should never be thought vexatious. Barnes turns this into a rule of the ministry, whose work is not only to impart truths not known before but largely to bring known ones back to recollection, since even true Christians let them slip. Henry makes the same point of the minister first: if ministers are negligent in their work the people can hardly be expected to be diligent in theirs, and he takes the old title of the Lord's remembrancers in both senses, of reminding the people of the promises and of putting God in mind of his engagements.

One phrase is disputed outright. Ellicott calls the present truth a translation misleading through its very literalness, the three Greek words being exactly represented while the sense is misrepresented, and denies that it means the truth now under discussion. Wesley gives precisely that sense — the truth which I am now declaring — so the two stand opposed on the same three words.

The verse about the tabernacle divides them further, and the division is about what is being said. Ellicott holds the received English wide of the mark and says only the earliest English version is right: the putting off of the tabernacle will be done swiftly, soon over once it begins, so the point is not the nearness of the end but its manner, which would allow no deathbed exhortations and made it necessary to speak in good time. Calvin gives the same literal rendering, short is the putting away of this tabernacle. Robertson allows both senses, soon or sudden, and says either agrees with the urgency, whether the death was felt to be near or violent or both. Barnes takes the plain sense and denies any revelation behind it, the writer being old. Clarke and Wesley both think a fresh intimation likely, Clarke adding that the prediction had fixed the death for old age and that being now aged he might fairly infer the rest.

On death itself Calvin draws the doctrine, that we are taught here how much death differs from perdition, and that we dread it too much because we do not consider how fading this life is; it is a departing from the world to remove elsewhere, to the Lord. Gill piles up the same figures, the putting off of a garment, the unpinning of a tent, a removal from a tent to a palace.

What the closing promise means is left open by the one who examines it. Ellicott lists the conjectures — this letter itself, copies of it distributed, further letters, the commissioning of an evangelist to write a Gospel, the instructing of faithful men — and says there seems to be nothing either for or against any of them. Barnes and Clarke both take it of the writings, Clarke asking whether the endeavour is not seen in these two epistles, and adding a classical parallel in which a philosopher, asked how he would be buried, answered that his friends might do as they pleased if they could catch him. Robertson notices what the word for decease carries: it is the word used on the mount of transfiguration for the departure of Christ, and the writer was there.
16:
What fables are being denied is answered four ways, and one of the answers is an argument. Clarke takes them for the heathen tales of gods appearing on earth in human form, and supports it from the last word of the verse: the mysteries staged such appearances, and those admitted to the innermost show were called beholders, which is the very term used here of the apostles. Gill allows both Jewish and Gentile fables and inclines the same way, noting that the word is the one used of the metamorphoses of the gods and that a transfiguration is about to be described. Wesley says simply, like those common among the heathens. Ellicott refuses to name any: the negative makes the statement general, and though heathen mythology, Jewish speculation, early Gnostic systems and apocryphal gospels have all been proposed, we cannot be sure any particular set is meant.

Two turn the denial into a positive argument. Barnes contrasts the manner of proof, the doctrine here resting not on the weak and sophistical reasoning by which Greek opinions were defended but on the personal observation of competent witnesses. Wesley argues from motive instead: if the account of Christ were their own invention, then imposing on the world a lie which by its nature no human power could defend, at the cost of life and everything else, and only to enrage Jews and Gentiles alike against them, would be not cunning at all but the greatest folly men could commit. Henry states the same conclusion positively, that this way of salvation is the counsel of God and no contrivance of men endeavouring by craft to deceive. Calvin gives the reason for raising the question at all, that it takes courage to labour in a matter one knows to be certain, and that men persevere when they are sure of the issue of their calling; and he notes that one memorable example has been chosen out of many.

The seventeenth verse divides two of them over a single pair of nouns. Ellicott holds that honour and glory both refer to the voice from heaven, and calls it forced and unnatural to take the first of the voice and the second of the light shining from Christ's body, since nothing has been said of that light. Clarke takes exactly the view Ellicott rejects, referring the honour to the words spoken and the glory to the altered countenance and the raiment white and glistening, each confirming the other; and Wesley follows him, glossing the glory as a shining above the brightness of the sun. Gill guards the sense from a different side, that the honour was not received as by an inferior from a superior nor added to an essential glory that admits no addition, but was declarative, the Father testifying what belonged to the Son while an external glory was put upon the son of man.

The remaining notes are structural and doctrinal. Robertson observes that the sentence has no finite verb and is left unfinished, the construction changing after the parenthesis of the next verse. Calvin explains why the display was needed, that the authority of the voice might be the more solemn, God having always added tokens of his presence to his words rather than letting them merely sound in the air. Cyril draws the practical consequence from the words themselves: the Father was well pleased in the Son, and a man who is not also well pleased in him has not life, so that whoever would show piety toward God must worship the Son, since otherwise the Father does not accept his service. Barnes adds that those who heard the voice could not doubt afterwards, and never did.
19:
One comparative adjective divides them further than anything else in the letter, and the question is what the prophetic word is being called surer than. Henry takes it at face value and says the apostle intimates that this second proof is stronger and more convincing than the first — that prophecy outweighs the vision on the mount. Gill sets out the alternatives and finds them all unsatisfactory: some make it surer than the cunningly devised fables, which he refuses, since writings of no authority whatever are not fit to be compared with the sacred ones; the comparison plainly lies rather between prophecy and the testimony of men who saw and heard the majesty of Christ, and how prophecy should be surer evidence than such testimony is hard to see, so that everyone rejects that sense, though by different roads. Barnes catalogues the roads: some deny that any comparison is intended and take the words to mean only that the word of prophecy is very sure; others hold that the prophecies, having been confirmed by the advent itself, are surer now than when they were uttered; and one great translator simply dropped the comparative and rendered it a firm prophetic word.

Clarke settles it by the lexicon rather than by the sense. The adjective, he says, means confirmed, and he proves the usage from five places in the New Testament where the related verb plainly bears it, so that the clause is to be read we have the prophetic doctrine more confirmed — which removes the ambiguity altogether, since the transfiguration confirmed the prophecies rather than being weighed against them. Wesley gives the same in a phrase, more confirmed by that display of his glorious majesty. Robertson agrees that the scene confirmed the messianic prophecies, and adds that those who make the prophetic word a surer proof of Christ's deity than the transfiguration take the less likely view — which is precisely Henry's view. Ellicott prefers the same rendering, notes that only one English version has it, observes that the expression occurs nowhere else in the New Testament and that an early Roman writer uses it of a quotation probably drawn from some uncanonical book of prophecies, and then admits that the sense of the whole sentence is not quite clear. Calvin closes off one escape: those who take the comparative for a positive have not considered the context sufficiently.

On who is meant by we, Calvin and Wesley agree against the narrower reading. Calvin says it takes in the other teachers and their disciples too, the apostles having the prophets as patrons of their doctrine and the faithful seeking from them a confirmation of the gospel; and he thinks the Jewish readers, familiar with the prophets, are chiefly in view. Wesley says the writer speaks in the name of all Christians, and that he cites no particular passage but the entire testimony of Moses, Isaiah and the rest, which is one word and everywhere consistent with itself.

The figure at the end is drawn out by Wesley more than by anyone. The lamp shines in a dark place, and the place is one with neither light nor window — such, he says, was the whole world anciently, except the little spot where this lamp shone; the dawning of the day is the breaking through of the full gospel light, and the difference between a lamp and the daylight is the difference between the two Testaments; the morning star is Christ himself, rising in the heart. Robertson keeps to the grammar of the same clause, taking the participle as holding the mind upon the thing, with the lamp in the same case. Gill and Henry both understand the prophetic word of the writings of the Old Testament concerning Christ, Henry listing what is foretold there of his Godhead, incarnation, power and coming.
20:
Barnes opens by conceding that the phrase about private interpretation has produced as much diversity and as much discussion as perhaps any expression in the New Testament, and that expositors have still reached no general agreement about it. Ellicott shows why: the noun occurs nowhere else in the New Testament, though the related verb means to expound, and the adjective may mean either private or its own, so that three constructions are open — one turning on the readers of prophecy and one on its source. Robertson decides the question and names the party he decides it against: the clause means that no prophecy comes out of private disclosure, not private interpretation, and the warning is not against personal exegesis, as one communion has argued, but against upstart prophets who speak with no impulse from God. Clarke arrives at the same place by the lexicon, since the noun can also mean impulse, and takes that to be the best sense here, so that prophecy proceeds from no calculation or conjecture and no private impulse of the prophet's own mind. Calvin reports the other reading as the one almost everybody gives — that we must not rush headlong on Scripture trusting our own understanding, the Spirit who spoke by the prophets being the only true interpreter of himself — and calls the doctrine in it true and useful. Wesley makes God himself the interpreter, the prophecy being nobody's own word and the interpretation of things till then unknown belonging to God and not to the prophet.

The next verse settles the matter for all of them, and Ellicott brings out the figure hidden in the Greek. The verb rendered came is the same word used twice already of the voice borne from heaven, and it is the same word rendered moved at the end of this verse, so that there is an antithesis English can hardly keep: prophecy was not brought in by men, but men were brought to utter it by the Spirit. He corrects two other things at once, that the sense is not at any time rather than in old time, an error he traces to a single English version, and that a reading of very high authority gives instead men spoke from God, moved by the Holy Ghost, which he prefers.

How far the prophets were themselves involved then divides them sharply. Clarke takes the participle at its strongest: they were carried away out of themselves and out of the whole region of human knowledge, the Spirit dictating what they should speak without their knowing anything of the matter, so that the words stood so far above their own understanding that they did not know the intent of them and had to search what manner of time was signified. Wesley agrees in a phrase, that they were purely passive. Calvin denies precisely this. They were moved, he says, not in the sense that they were bereaved of mind, as the Gentiles imagined of their own prophets, but because they dared announce nothing of their own and obediently followed the Spirit as their guide, who ruled in their mouth as in his own sanctuary. Robertson keeps to the tense, that they were moved from time to time and that what they then did was to speak from God.

Two smaller notes close the chapter. Barnes observes that the noun stands without the article, so that what is said holds of prophecy in general and indeed of everything the prophets taught, whether it concerned future events or not. Gill remarks that the Jews call the Scriptures the prophecy by way of eminence, from the subject matter of the sacred word.
